examples.en: We decided to hold a family meeting this weekend.

examples.ko: 우리는 가족회의에서 여름 여행 장소를 정했어요.
examples.en: We chose our summer trip destination at a family meeting.
The family meeting starts after dinner.
A family meeting was suddenly called, so I felt a bit nervous.

examples.ko: 가족회의 때 모두 자기 의견을 말해요.
examples.en: At family meetings, everyone says their own opinion.
In our house, we decide big matters through a family meeting.

explain: '가족회의를 열다/하다'처럼 말해요. 회사의 딱딱한 회의와 달리 집에서 편하게 의견을 나누는 자리라는 느낌이에요. 이사, 여행, 용돈처럼 가족이 함께 정할 일에 잘 어울려요.
explain_en: You say it as '가족회의를 열다/하다'. Unlike a stiff business meeting, it feels like a relaxed time at home to share opinions. It suits things a family decides together, such as moving, trips or allowances.

examples.en: My father goes to the golf course every Sunday.
The golf course in our town is in the mountains.
The scenery at this golf course is really nice.
It takes an hour by car to get to the golf course.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 회사 사람들과 골프장을 예약했어요.
examples.en: I booked the golf course with my coworkers for this weekend.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와서 골프장이 문을 닫았어요.
examples.en: It rained a lot, so the golf course closed.

explain: 골프는 '치다'와 함께 써서 '골프를 치다'라고 해요. 골프장에서 한 바퀴 도는 것을 '라운딩'이라고도 하고, 골프장 이름 뒤에는 'CC'를 자주 붙여요. '골프 치러 가다'처럼 목적을 말할 때는 '골프장' 없이도 돼요.
explain_en: Golf pairs with '치다' (hit), so you say '골프를 치다'. Playing a round at the course is also called '라운딩', and course names often end in 'CC'. For purpose you can say '골프 치러 가다' (go to play golf) without mentioning the course.

examples.ko: 월급이 매달 하순에 들어와서 그전에는 돈이 빠듯해요.
examples.en: My pay comes in late each month, so money is tight before that.

examples.ko: 그전 같으면 이런 일에 화를 냈을 거예요.
examples.en: In the past, I would have gotten angry about something like this.

examples.ko: 그전과 비교하면 요즘은 훨씬 여유가 있어요.
examples.en: Compared to before, I have much more breathing room these days.
I sometimes think of the neighborhood where I lived before.
I have changed a lot from who I was before.

examples.ko: 그전엔 매일 걸어서 출근했는데 지금은 차로 가요.
examples.en: I used to walk to work every day, but now I go by car.

explain: '예전'이 막연히 오래전을 가리킨다면 '그전'은 앞에서 말한 일이나 때보다 앞선 시간을 가리켜요. '그전에는, 그전 같으면'처럼 지금과 비교할 때 자주 나와요. '그 전'처럼 띄어 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: While '예전' vaguely points to long ago, '그전' points to a time before the event or time just mentioned. It often appears when comparing with now, as in '그전에는' and '그전 같으면'. You will also see it written as '그 전'.

examples.en: At night the temperature drops.
Interest rates have gone down lately, so loans got easier.

examples.ko: 시험이 너무 어려우면 평균 점수가 낮아질 수 있어요.
examples.en: If the test is too hard, the average score can go down.
When you press the button, the desk slowly lowers.

examples.ko: 목소리가 낮아지면 화가 났다는 느낌이 들어요.
examples.en: When someone's voice gets low, it feels like they are angry.

examples.ko: 겨울이 되자 바닷물 온도가 많이 낮아졌어요.
examples.en: When winter came, the sea water temperature dropped a lot.

explain: '높아지다'의 반대말이고, 높이·온도·점수·수준처럼 위아래로 재는 것에 두루 써요. 소리는 '작아지다'와 달리 '낮아지다'라고 하면 음의 높낮이가 내려간다는 뜻이 돼요. 값이 내려갈 때는 '싸지다'나 '내려가다'도 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is the opposite of '높아지다' and works for anything measured up and down, such as height, temperature, scores and level. For voices, '낮아지다' means the pitch goes down, unlike '작아지다', which means quieter. For prices, people also say '싸지다' or '내려가다'.

examples.en: Washing my hands in warm water warms me up.
I drink a glass of warm water every morning.
No hot water comes out of the tap.
Soaking my feet in warm water relieved my fatigue.
Please mix hot and cold water half and half.
On cold days, a hot shower is the best.

explain: 반대말은 '찬물'이에요. 말할 때는 '뜨거운 물'이나 '따뜻한 물'을 더 자주 쓰고, 안내문이나 설명서에서는 '온수'를 많이 봐요. '더운물'은 샤워, 세수처럼 씻을 때 자연스럽게 나와요.
explain_en: The opposite is '찬물' (cold water). In speech people often say '뜨거운 물' or '따뜻한 물', and signs or manuals often use '온수'. '더운물' comes up naturally when washing, such as showering or washing your face.

examples.en: My daughter enters elementary school this year.
My daughter wakes me up every morning.
I went to the park with my daughter.
I bought a new bike for my daughter.
The neighbors' little girl said hello and passed by.
When I think of my daughter, I get energy.

explain: 자기 딸을 남에게 말할 때 '딸'보다 부드럽게 들려서 '딸아이'를 많이 써요. 아들은 '아들아이'도 쓰지만 보통 그냥 '아들'이라고 해요. 남의 딸을 높여 말할 때는 '따님'이라고 해요.
explain_en: Parents often say 딸아이 when talking about their own daughter to others since it sounds softer than 딸. For a son, 아들아이 exists but people usually just say 아들. To honor someone else's daughter, use 따님.

examples.en: There's a wedding tomorrow, so I got my hair done today.
Which salon do you go to for your hair these days?
I'm going to get my hair done at the salon this weekend.
Getting my hair done for the first time in a while feels really good.
I went to the salon to get my hair done before the interview.

examples.ko: 친구와 같이 머리하고 나서 사진을 찍었어요.
examples.en: After getting our hair done together, my friend and I took photos.

explain: 커트인지 파마인지 염색인지 말하지 않고 두루 쓸 때 편한 입말이에요. 구체적으로 말하려면 '머리를 자르다', '파마하다', '염색하다'를 써요. 집에서 머리를 씻고 말리는 건 '머리를 감다', '머리를 말리다'라서 '머리하다'가 아니에요.
explain_en: A casual word for visiting a salon without saying whether it's a cut, perm, or dye. To be specific, say '머리를 자르다' (cut), '파마하다' (perm), or '염색하다' (dye). Washing or drying your hair at home is '머리를 감다' or '머리를 말리다', not '머리하다'.

examples.en: I had barley rice bibimbap for lunch.

examples.ko: 보리밥에 나물을 넣고 고추장으로 비벼 먹어요.
examples.en: I put namul on the barley rice and mix it with gochujang.
This restaurant is famous for its tasty barley rice.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 할머니가 보리밥을 자주 해 주셨어요.
examples.en: When I was little, my grandmother often made barley rice for me.
Barley rice has more chewiness than plain white rice.
For my health, I switched to barley rice.

explain: 쌀로만 지은 '쌀밥', 여러 곡식을 섞은 '잡곡밥'과 구별해서 말해요. 식당에서는 '보리밥 정식'이나 '보리밥집'처럼 나물과 함께 나오는 메뉴로 자주 봐요.
explain_en: It is distinguished from '쌀밥' (rice only) and '잡곡밥' (mixed grains). At restaurants you often see it as a set meal served with namul, such as '보리밥 정식' or at a '보리밥집'.

examples.en: A spring breeze is blowing and I feel good.
I opened the window and felt the spring breeze.
The spring breeze is warm, but it sometimes blows pollen too.
My hair got all tangled because of the spring wind.
While I was walking, my hat blew off in the spring wind.

examples.ko: 오늘은 봄바람처럼 부드러운 노래를 듣고 싶어요.
examples.en: Today I want to listen to a song as soft as a spring breeze.

explain: 봄바람은 봄에 부는 따뜻하고 부드러운 바람이에요. 이른 봄에 꽃을 시샘하듯 부는 쌀쌀한 바람은 '꽃샘바람'이라고 해요. '봄바람이 불다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: 봄바람 is the warm, soft wind of spring. The chilly wind of early spring, as if jealous of the flowers, is called 꽃샘바람. Say '봄바람이 불다'.

examples.en: My aunt brought kimchi to our house.
At the holiday I met my aunt and greeted her.
I went to the market with my aunt.
My aunt cooks really well.

examples.ko: 숙모 댁에 사촌이 세 명 있어요.
examples.en: There are three cousins at my aunt's house.
Yesterday I gave my aunt a birthday present.

explain: 숙모는 아버지의 남동생 아내예요. 어머니의 남자 형제 아내는 '외숙모', 아버지의 여자 형제는 '고모', 어머니의 여자 형제는 '이모'라서 서로 구분해서 불러요. 직접 부를 때는 '숙모님'이라고 해요.
explain_en: 숙모 is the wife of your father's younger brother. Your mother's brother's wife is 외숙모, your father's sister is 고모 and your mother's sister is 이모, so each has its own word. To address her directly, say '숙모님'.

examples.ko: 우리 수업이 아침 아홉 시에 시작돼요.
examples.en: Our class starts at nine in the morning.

examples.ko: 우리가 도착했을 때 영화가 벌써 시작됐어요.
examples.en: The movie had already started when we arrived.
The new semester will start tomorrow.
Before the game starts, the players greet each other.
The meeting started, so I turned off my phone.

examples.ko: 방학이 시작되면 가족과 여행을 가고 싶어요.
examples.en: When vacation starts, I want to travel with my family.

explain: '시작하다'는 사람이 일을 여는 것이고, '시작되다'는 시간이 되어 저절로 열리는 것이에요. 수업·영화·회의·방학처럼 주어가 사람이 아닌 일일 때 '시작되다'를 써요. 짝말로 '이야기가 시작되다', '새로운 하루가 시작되다'도 자주 나와요.
explain_en: '시작하다' is for a person who starts something; '시작되다' is for something that starts on its own when the time comes. Use it when the subject is an event, not a person: class, a movie, a meeting, vacation. Common phrases include 'a new day begins' and 'the story begins'.

dis.h: something begins by itself, no doer

p.n: The other verb needs a doer and an object (수업을 시작해요), so the same sentence cannot simply swap.

examples.en: Hotel check-out is until noon.
Pack all your things before check-out.
I asked whether I could check out late.
I returned the key card as I checked out.

examples.ko: 체크아웃 시간이 지나면 추가 요금이 붙어요.
examples.en: If you go past check-out time, an extra fee is added.

examples.ko: 공항에 가야 해서 일찍 체크아웃할 거예요.
examples.en: I have to go to the airport, so I'll check out early.

explain: 반대말은 '체크인'이에요. 호텔이나 숙소에서 방을 비우고 나가는 일이고, 일상에서는 '방을 빼다'라는 말도 써요. 시간은 '체크아웃 시간', 장소는 '프런트에서 체크아웃' 같이 말해요.
explain_en: The opposite is '체크인'. It means leaving the room at a hotel or lodging, and in everyday talk people also say '방을 빼다'. People say '체크아웃 시간' (check-out time) and '프런트에서 체크아웃' (check out at the front desk).

examples.ko: 한국어 초급반에서 한 달째 공부하고 있어요.
examples.en: I've been studying in a beginner Korean class for a month.
Lessons in the beginner class go slowly.
I signed up for a beginner swimming class.
Everyone in the beginner class works hard.
After taking the test, I was placed in the beginner class.
I finished the beginner class and moved up to intermediate.

explain: '초급반, 중급반, 고급반'이 세 단계로 짝이 돼요. 어학원이나 운동 강습에서 자주 쓰는 말이에요. 반을 옮길 때는 '올라가다', 배정할 때는 '배정되다'와 같이 나와요.
explain_en: '초급반, 중급반, 고급반' (beginner, intermediate, advanced) make a set of three levels. It's common at language schools and exercise classes. It goes with '올라가다' (move up) when changing classes and '배정되다' (be placed).

examples.en: Dust got in and the inside of my nose itches.
I caught a cold and my nose is completely blocked.
I feel like something got inside my nose.
In dry winter, the inside of your nose easily dries out.
The doctor examined the inside of my nose.
The spicy smell rushes all the way up into my nose.

explain: '코'와 '속'이 합쳐진 말이라 소리 낼 때 [콛쏙]처럼 '쏙'으로 세게 나요. 감기, 먼지, 건조함처럼 코 안쪽이 불편할 때 자주 써요.
explain_en: It is '코' plus '속', and it is pronounced [콛쏙] with a tense 'ssok' sound. It is used when something feels uncomfortable inside the nose, such as with a cold, dust or dryness.

examples.en: When the green light comes on, we cross the street.
The crosswalk signal changed to green.
The green light is blinking, so don't run.
I am waiting for the green light at the crosswalk.
You stop at the red light and go at the green light.
The light was green but a car didn't stop, so I was startled.

explain: 신호등의 초록색도 한국어에서는 보통 '파란불'이라고 말해요. 반대는 '빨간불'이고, 신호는 '켜지다/바뀌다'와 같이 써요.

phrases.en: The new business finally got the go-ahead.
phrases.nuance_ko: 일이 잘 풀릴 조짐이 보인다는 비유예요. 반대로 '빨간불이 켜지다'는 문제가 생겼다는 뜻이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: A figure of speech meaning things are starting to look promising. The opposite, '빨간불이 켜지다', means trouble has appeared.

explain_en: Even though the traffic signal is green, Korean speakers usually call it '파란불'. The opposite is '빨간불', and it goes with verbs like '켜지다' and '바뀌다'.

en: part-time job; side job; student job; moonlighting

examples.en: During vacation I work part-time at a cafe.

examples.ko: 방학 때 할 파트타임 일을 구하고 있어요.
examples.en: I am looking for a part-time job to do during vacation.
I only work part-time on weekends.
Since it is part-time, my schedule is fairly flexible.
This shop is hiring part-time staff.
I earn my pocket money from my part-time pay.

explain: 학생이나 젊은 사람이 일할 때는 '알바(아르바이트)'라는 말을 더 많이 해요. '파트타임'은 시간제로 일한다는 근무 방식을 말할 때 잘 쓰고, 반대는 '풀타임'이에요.
explain_en: When students or young people talk about such work, they more often say '알바' (아르바이트). '파트타임' fits when you mean the working style of limited hours, and its opposite is '풀타임'.
